Yes. The MCP testing ecosystem now exists, but it is fragmented. No single framework covers protocol compliance, product semantics, authorization, client compatibility, security, performance, and LLM tool selection.

For Skillplane, I would keep the existing TypeScript/Vitest foundation and add targeted external gates—not replace it with another framework.

## Useful MCP testing tools

| Tool | Best use | Important limitation |
|---|---|---|
| [Official MCP Conformance Framework](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/conformance) | Protocol/version/wire-schema compliance, known-failure baselines, CI | Some scenarios require special test tools; authenticated server mode is still awkward |
| [Official MCP Inspector](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector) | Web, CLI, and TUI debugging; ad-hoc host compatibility checks | Primarily exploratory, not product regression coverage |
| [MCP Test Harness](https://github.com/vaquarkhan/mcp-test-harness) | Python-authored deterministic tool tests, snapshots, performance, reports | Young, Python-only authoring, not official conformance |
| [Bellwether](https://github.com/dotsetlabs/bellwether) | Tool/resource/prompt schema drift and golden-output detection | Very low external adoption so far |
| [MCP-Jest](https://github.com/ReallyArtificial/mcp-jest) | Node-oriented discovery, snapshots, tool assertions | Community project; evaluate maturity before depending on it |
| [MCP Testing Framework](https://github.com/L-Qun/mcp-testing-framework) | Testing whether different LLMs choose the correct tool and arguments | Stochastic and model-dependent; unsuitable as the primary PR gate |
| [Snyk Agent Scan](https://github.com/snyk/agent-scan) | Tool poisoning, prompt injection, shadowing, toxic-flow scanning | Security scanner, not functional testing; may send metadata to Snyk |

A strong real-world pattern is the one used by GitHub’s own MCP server: unit tests, table-driven behavioral tests, E2E tests, and a checked-in snapshot for every tool schema. Missing snapshots fail CI rather than silently establishing a new baseline. [GitHub MCP server testing strategy](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server/blob/main/docs/testing.md).

## What `mcp-test-harness` exactly does

It is a custom Python test runner that follows pytest naming conventions. Consumer tests look like pytest, but `mcp-test` performs its own discovery, fixture injection, scheduling, retries, and reporting.

It:

- Starts a local stdio MCP server or connects to SSE/Streamable HTTP.
- Performs initialization through the official Python MCP SDK.
- Injects an `mcp_server` session into `test_*.py` functions.
- Tests tools, resources, prompts, capabilities, schemas, errors, latency and throughput.
- Supports response snapshots and a full tool/resource/prompt manifest snapshot.
- Accepts static HTTP headers, including a bearer token.
- Generates JSON, JUnit, HTML, SARIF and PR summaries.
- Tracks advertised-versus-tested tools.
- Provides record/generate helpers and synthetic fault injection.
- Has a GitHub Action and container distribution.

I independently installed version `4.0.1` from its source and ran its minimal real-stdio dogfood flow. It passed `1/1`.

There are several significant boundaries:

- It does **not** execute the official MCP conformance suite. Its “conformance levels” are project-defined scores based on its own tests.
- It does **not** perform Skillplane’s OAuth browser/PKCE flow. It can only use a token supplied through headers.
- Its authorization helper uses one session with allowed versus denied arguments. True principal separation still requires separately authenticated sessions.
- Its “chaos” layer synthetically delays, truncates or alters client-visible calls; it is not database, R2, network or Cloudflare failure injection.
- A missing manifest baseline is automatically created and passes. For CI, that means deleting the baseline could inadvertently green-light a change unless a separate missing-file or dirty-worktree check exists. [Manifest implementation](https://github.com/vaquarkhan/mcp-test-harness/blob/v4.0.1/src/mcp_test_harness/manifest_gate.py#L224-L250).
- It currently pins Python MCP SDK `<2`, and its GitHub adoption is still tiny—5 stars and no forks when checked. That is a risk signal, not proof of poor quality.

My verdict: it is a credible optional black-box/nightly sidecar for Skillplane, especially for reports, schema snapshots and latency checks. I would not make it Skillplane’s primary testing foundation or migrate the existing Vitest suites into Python.

If piloted, pin `4.0.1`, use a short-lived staging token, use read-only credentials initially, require the baseline file to already exist, and do not treat its badge as official spec compliance.

## Skillplane’s present position

Skillplane is already fairly strong:

- The root [package scripts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/package.json:25) expose unit, integration, security, recovery, performance, MCP conformance, MCP E2E and production gates.
- Its [custom MCP contract suite](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/mcp/tests/conformance/mcp.conformance.test.ts:49) checks initialization, 27 tools, schemas, annotations, structured/text parity, media negotiation, protocol errors and Linear’s catalog budget.
- Across `mcp/tests`, there are currently 47 MCP-focused test cases covering read, mutation, lifecycle, tenancy, OAuth, service credentials, pagination, replay, auditing and storage failures.
- The [production MCP verifier](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/scripts/test-mcp-production.mjs:36) checks the live server identity, all 27 tool names and several read flows.

The important gaps are:

1. `test:mcp:conformance` is custom Vitest—not official conformance. I would rename it `test:mcp:contract` and introduce a separate `test:mcp:spec`.

2. Tool inventory is hardcoded, but complete schemas are not snapshotted. A parameter becoming required, a type narrowing, or an output field disappearing could escape the existing catalog assertions.

3. There is no `.github/workflows` directory in the checkout. The tests exist, but no checked-in merge enforcement is visible. External branch protection may exist, but it cannot be inferred locally.

4. Production verification explicitly rejects `spk_` agent credentials. Local service-credential tests exist, but the real staging/production transport path lacks an agent-key canary.

5. SDK success does not prove host success. Codex, Claude, Linear and Inspector can differ around OAuth, catalog size, structured output, caller attribution and refresh behavior.

6. Deterministic tests do not measure whether models choose the right one of 27 tools. Because MCP tools are model-controlled and descriptions/schema guide selection, this needs a separate statistical evaluation layer. [MCP tool specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools).

## Recommended release system

| Gate | What should block |
|---|---|
| Every PR | Existing unit/integration/security suites; canonical tool manifest diff; output-schema validation; official generic conformance; every tool represented in the coverage matrix |
| Staging | Real OAuth PKCE and `spk_` sessions; wrong audience; expiry/revocation; scope and role matrix; cross-workspace denial; disposable mutation/replay/audit flows |
| Nightly | Multiple real MCP clients; malformed-input/property fuzzing; concurrent mutations; cold-start and p95/p99 performance; R2/DB/audit failure injection |
| Model evaluation | Prompts asserting expected tool, arguments and “do not call” cases across pinned models; initially advisory, later thresholded |
| Production deploy | Read-only OAuth and `spk_` canaries, catalog digest, one golden retrieve/search flow, audit evidence and automatic rollback criteria |

The highest-value immediate work is therefore:

1. Add an enforced CI workflow.
2. Separate product-contract tests from official spec conformance.
3. Add fail-closed, checked-in snapshots of all 27 complete tool definitions.
4. Generate a per-tool coverage matrix for success, malformed input, scope denial, tenant denial, replay/idempotency, audit and live canary.
5. Add the missing real `spk_` staging canary.
6. Add real-client and LLM-selection evaluations after the deterministic gates are solid.

No Skillplane files were changed during this investigation.

Yes—McpFn would likely pay off long-term, but only with a strict architectural boundary:

- McpFn should be the shared MCP runtime, contract, compatibility, and regression layer.
- `@mcpfn/datafn` should be an optional adapter.
- McpFn should not become “DataFn exposed over MCP by default.”
- McpFn should invoke official conformance tooling, not implement its own version of the MCP specification.

## My recommendation

| Idea | Verdict | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|
| McpFn for MCP testing/regression | Strong yes | Focus on contracts, semantic regressions, CI and reusable transports |
| McpFn as a shared MCP runtime | Strong yes | Use the official SDK underneath |
| `@mcpfn/datafn` for low-effort tools | Yes | Explicit allowlisted exposure through DataFn’s complete policy pipeline |
| Automatically exposing every DataFn resource | No | Too easy to leak fields and create unstable, low-quality tools |
| Replacing Skillplane’s curated MCP tools with generated DataFn CRUD | No | Skillplane’s MCP is a domain API, not a database facade |

## What the Superfunctions repositories show

I inspected the `next`, `dev`, ApiFn readiness, BillFn, SF-8, SFN-15, and SF-35 worktrees. The relevant architectural source of truth is currently `next`.

The `superfunctions-dev` checkout contains promising DataFn application/plugin work, but it is part of a very large uncommitted integration stack. The ApiFn production-readiness worktree has no meaningful ApiFn source delta from `next`; the other worktrees are unrelated to McpFn. Therefore I would not build McpFn against the dirty `dev` extension API yet.

There are four strong reasons for McpFn already inside Superfunctions.

### 1. MCP implementation has already fragmented

There are currently three substantially different implementations:

- [LangFn’s MCP server](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/langfn/typescript/src/mcp/server.ts:6) implements a small custom protocol surface rather than using the official SDK.
- [MemoryFn’s MCP server](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/memoryfn/typescript/src/mcp/server.ts:1) uses the official SDK, but its package does not directly declare that SDK dependency; root hoisting conceals the packaging problem.
- [ProbeFn’s MCP server](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/probefn/packages/mcp-server/src/server.ts:434) implements framing, initialization, tools and protocol handling manually and is tied to an older protocol model.

That duplication alone justifies a shared McpFn runtime. It would remove protocol code from domain functions and prevent every function from independently chasing MCP changes.

That matters especially now: the official TypeScript SDK documents materially different “2025-era” and `2026-07-28` protocol behavior. A home-grown server abstraction will age quickly. [Official protocol-version documentation](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/blob/main/docs/protocol-versions.md).

### 2. ApiFn contains the right product pattern

[ApiFn](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/apifn/README.md:3) already establishes a good pattern:

- deterministic contract generation;
- validation;
- breaking-change classification;
- declarative collections;
- machine-readable reports;
- stable CLI exit semantics;
- reusable CI enforcement.

Its [diff engine](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/apifn/core/src/diff/diff.ts:30) and [CI workflow](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/apifn/.github/workflows/api-check.yml:107) are the conceptual model for McpFn.

But McpFn cannot simply rename OpenAPI concepts:

- Tool descriptions and titles influence model selection.
- Safety annotations affect host behavior.
- Tool inventory size affects context budgets.
- Auth, protocol negotiation and transport support are part of compatibility.
- A JSON-Schema-compatible change can still be a model-facing regression.

McpFn therefore needs three diff classes:

1. **Breaking:** removed tool, newly required input, narrowed input, removed output, tighter scope, dropped protocol/transport.
2. **Additive:** new tool, optional input, compatible output addition.
3. **Behavioral review:** descriptions, titles, annotations, tool grouping and catalog-size changes.

That third category is the MCP-specific piece ApiFn does not need.

### 3. DataFn does not yet expose a safe plugin boundary for this

The current [DataFn plugin contract](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/datafn/core/src/types.ts:255) consists primarily of before/after query, mutation and sync hooks. It cannot declare MCP tools.

More importantly, the public [DataFn server surface](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/datafn/server/src/server.ts:247) does not offer a transport-neutral:

```ts
query(context, input)
mutate(context, input)
transact(context, input)
search(context, input)
```

API. The complete validation, namespace, authorization, field-permission, idempotency and hook pipeline remains inside HTTP route handlers.

The dirty `dev` worktree introduces a useful [DatafnApp abstraction](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions-dev/datafn/server/src/app.ts:23) and composable routes, but those plugin routes receive raw database/schema access. An MCP adapter built on that interface could accidentally bypass DataFn’s normal security pipeline.

The prerequisite should be a shared `DatafnExecutor` or `DatafnService`:

```text
HTTP transport ───────────────┐
                              v
DataFnApp → DatafnExecutor → validation/authz/namespace/hooks/database
                              ^
@mcpfn/datafn → MCP tools ────┘
```

Then both HTTP and MCP execute through the same policy path.

You can still present it ergonomically as a “DataFn plugin,” but internally `@mcpfn/datafn` should be an adapter consuming DataFn—not a hook with raw database access.

### 4. Skillplane proves why generation must be selective

Skillplane’s MCP is not a thin DataFn facade.

Its [tool registry](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/mcp/src/server.ts:118) contains 27 curated tools with intentionally written descriptions, schemas and annotations. Its [runtime](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/mcp/src/tools/shared.ts:29) also handles:

- credential-derived identity;
- caller declarations;
- role authorization;
- immutable skill/version resolution;
- cursor binding;
- audit records;
- asset/download grants;
- domain-specific errors;
- structured/text response parity.

Meanwhile, Skillplane’s [DataFn server](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/datafn/src/server.ts:44) is deliberately read-only, tenant-scoped and resource-allowlisted. Its [security test](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/datafn/tests/security/tenant-foundation.test.ts:4) explicitly keeps credentials, storage locators and audit data outside DataFn.

Therefore:

- McpFn should replace Skillplane’s transport/registration boilerplate and strengthen its contract testing.
- Skillplane’s existing domain handlers should remain explicit.
- The DataFn adapter may generate a few safe read-model tools.
- It should not generate replacements for Skillplane’s mutation, authorization, version-resolution or asset-delivery tools.

## What `mcp-test-harness` actually does

I source-inspected its current `4.0.1` main branch; I did not install or execute it.

[MCP Test Harness](https://github.com/vaquarkhan/mcp-test-harness) is a substantive Python test framework, not merely a smoke-test script. It provides:

- real stdio, SSE and Streamable HTTP sessions;
- Python `test_*.py` discovery;
- fixtures and assertions for tools, resources, prompts and capabilities;
- schema validation;
- response snapshots with masking;
- latency, throughput and idempotency assertions;
- security payloads and chaos experiments;
- parallel scheduling, retry/watch support;
- JSON, JUnit, HTML and SARIF reports;
- recording and generated test scaffolds;
- a deterministic MCP surface snapshot.

Its [manifest gate](https://github.com/vaquarkhan/mcp-test-harness/blob/main/src/mcp_test_harness/manifest_gate.py) captures protocol version, capabilities, tools, resources and prompts, then fails when the snapshot changes.

The limitations relevant to McpFn are:

- It is Python-first, while the current Superfunctions runtime/package ecosystem is primarily TypeScript and Turbo.
- Its manifest gate treats every difference as drift; it does not provide ApiFn-quality breaking/additive/behavioral classification.
- Its “Boot / Protocol / Covered / Secure / Resilient” conformance badge is the project’s own grading system. [Its grading implementation](https://github.com/vaquarkhan/mcp-test-harness/blob/main/src/mcp_test_harness/conformance.py).
- Its stateless conformance command currently runs a small targeted HTTP matrix; it is not the official full MCP conformance suite.
- It explicitly does not test whether models choose the correct tool.

I would use it as an optional black-box CI runner—especially for recording, chaos, performance and reports—but I would not make McpFn runtime depend on it.

The broader testing landscape currently includes:

- [Official MCP conformance](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/conformance): authoritative protocol/version/wire compatibility and expected-failure baselines.
- [Official MCP Inspector](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector): interactive exploration and debugging, useful locally but not sufficient as a regression gate.
- [MCP Test Harness](https://github.com/vaquarkhan/mcp-test-harness): deterministic functional/regression/performance testing.
- [MCP Testing Framework](https://github.com/L-Qun/mcp-testing-framework): model-driven evaluation of whether different LLMs select the right tools and arguments.

They solve different layers. A healthy Skillplane pipeline needs more than one.

## Suggested McpFn package shape

Following existing Superfunctions conventions:

```text
mcpfn/
  core/       @mcpfn/core
  testing/    @mcpfn/testing
  cli/        @mcpfn/cli
  datafn/     @mcpfn/datafn
```

Responsibilities:

- `@mcpfn/core`: thin official-SDK facade, tool registry, manifest generation, transports and common result/error conventions.
- `@mcpfn/testing`: in-memory clients, Vitest fixtures/matchers, semantic scenarios and compatibility rules.
- `@mcpfn/cli`: `validate`, `manifest`, `diff`, `test`, `conformance`.
- `@mcpfn/datafn`: explicit DataFn-to-tool exposure manifest.

The dependency direction should be:

```text
@mcpfn/datafn → @mcpfn/core + DataFn
DataFn         ✕ McpFn
```

DataFn should remain useful without MCP, and McpFn must support non-DataFn functions such as ProbeFn, LangFn and FileFn.

The DataFn adapter should require explicit declarations:

```ts
mcpfnDatafn({
  app,
  expose: {
    skills: {
      list: {
        name: "skills_list",
        description: "List skills visible to the authenticated workspace",
        fields: ["id", "slug", "name", "updatedAt"],
        filters: ["query", "status"],
        maxLimit: 50
      }
    }
  }
});
```

Required defaults:

- deny all resources unless explicitly exposed;
- reads only unless mutations are opted in;
- public tool names decoupled from DataFn resource names;
- explicit output projection and redaction;
- server-derived principal/namespace, never supplied as tool arguments;
- bounded filters, pagination and limits;
- idempotency required for writes;
- audit integration;
- tool-count and serialized catalog budgets;
- no general-purpose “execute DFQL” tool.

## Regression strategy for Skillplane

On every PR:

- McpFn manifest validation and compatibility diff.
- Official conformance for every supported protocol era/transport.
- Deterministic scenarios for all tools.
- Tenant, role, scope, audit and redaction matrices.
- Structured-content/text parity.
- Idempotency and optimistic-concurrency cases.
- Isolated package install/consumer tests to catch undeclared dependencies.

Nightly or pre-release:

- Real-host checks against Codex, Claude, Linear and other important clients.
- Tool-selection and argument-generation evaluations.
- Catalog/context-budget regression.
- Chaos, performance and retry tests.
- Staging production-auth canaries.

Skillplane’s existing [custom MCP conformance runner](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/scripts/run-mcp-conformance.mjs:15) is a useful semantic suite, but it currently runs one project-specific Vitest file. McpFn should preserve those assertions and add the official external runner—not replace one with the other.

## Adoption order

1. Run official conformance against LangFn, MemoryFn, ProbeFn and Skillplane and capture an honest baseline.
2. Build only `@mcpfn/core`, manifest/diff and a thin testing layer.
3. Migrate ProbeFn first; its private, hand-built MCP server is a good proving ground.
4. Migrate MemoryFn and fix isolated-package dependencies.
5. Migrate LangFn.
6. Extract the DataFn transport-neutral executor.
7. Build a read-only `@mcpfn/datafn` adapter.
8. Adopt McpFn’s runtime/testing in Skillplane while retaining its curated handlers.
9. Add generated DataFn mutations only after authorization, idempotency and audit equivalence are proven.

Bottom line: McpFn is a good long-term Superfunction because the repository already has enough MCP duplication and protocol drift to justify it. The DataFn adapter is also a good idea, but it should generate narrowly curated tools over a shared DataFn execution kernel. If “minimal effort” means “one explicit exposure manifest and no duplicated handler plumbing,” that is realistic. If it means “publish the DataFn schema automatically as MCP CRUD,” it will eventually create security, compatibility and tool-quality problems.

+# McpFn
+
+McpFn is the Superfunctions layer for building and keeping Model Context Protocol servers regression-free. It uses the official MCP SDK for protocol and transport behavior, then adds the application-level contracts that production MCP consumers need: validated tool definitions, deterministic manifests, compatibility diffs, semantic scenarios, and a safe DataFn adapter.
+
+## Packages
+
+| Package | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `@mcpfn/core` | Official-SDK server runtime, tool registry, result/error normalization, manifests, and compatibility diffing |
+| `@mcpfn/testing` | Official in-memory client, exact contract assertions, semantic scenarios, and official conformance orchestration |
+| `@mcpfn/datafn` | Deny-by-default generation of bounded MCP tools from a DataFn server executor |
+| `@mcpfn/cli` | `manifest`, `validate`, `diff`, `test`, and `conformance` commands with stable CI exit codes |
+
+McpFn is intentionally tool-focused in its first release. Resources, prompts, elicitation, sampling, tasks, and authorization-server discovery remain the responsibility of the official SDK or explicit application code until McpFn gives them the same contract and regression guarantees as tools.
+
+## Quick start
+
+```ts
+import {
+  McpFnRegistry,
+  createMcpFnServer,
+  structuredResult,
+} from "@mcpfn/core";
+
+const registry = new McpFnRegistry().register({
+  name: "skill_get",
+  description: "Resolve one published skill by slug.",
+  inputSchema: {
+    type: "object",
+    properties: { slug: { type: "string", minLength: 1 } },
+    required: ["slug"],
+    additionalProperties: false,
+  },
+  outputSchema: {
+    type: "object",
+    properties: { skill: { type: "object" } },
+    required: ["skill"],
+    additionalProperties: false,
+  },
+  annotations: {
+    readOnlyHint: true,
+    destructiveHint: false,
+    idempotentHint: true,
+    openWorldHint: false,
+  },
+  handler: async ({ slug }) =>
+    structuredResult({ skill: await resolvePublishedSkill(String(slug)) }),
+});
+
+const server = createMcpFnServer({
+  info: { name: "skillplane", version: "1.0.0" },
+  registry,
+  transports: ["stdio", "streamable-http"],
+});
+
+await server.serveStdio();
+```
+
+The handler receives only schema-valid arguments. If an output schema is declared, McpFn also validates `structuredContent` before returning it. Domain errors with a string `code` retain that code in the MCP error result.
+
+## Regression workflow
+
+Commit a manifest baseline and semantic scenarios with the MCP server:
+
+```sh
+mcpfn manifest ./src/mcp/server.ts --output ./mcpfn.manifest.json
+mcpfn validate ./mcpfn.manifest.json
+mcpfn diff ./mcpfn.manifest.json ./candidate.manifest.json --fail-on-behavioral
+mcpfn test ./src/mcp/server.ts ./tests/mcp.scenarios.ts --output ./mcpfn-report.json
+mcpfn conformance http://127.0.0.1:3000/mcp --suite active
+```
+
+The manifest catches tool inventory, schema, annotation, description, protocol-version, and transport changes. Scenarios catch business behavior. The official conformance runner catches wire-protocol behavior. None of those layers substitutes for the others.
+
+Run `npm run gate:mcpfn-release` from this repository for the complete package, example, migration, and packability gate.
+
+## DataFn boundary
+
+`@mcpfn/datafn` is useful when a domain operation really is a bounded projection of DataFn query/mutation semantics. A resource must be explicitly named, returned fields are fixed, filter/sort fields are allowlisted, and writes require explicit fields plus a caller-supplied `mutationId`. Authentication, namespace, actor, and `clientId` values come from trusted server context.
+
+Do not auto-publish an entire DataFn schema. Skillplane-style operations such as version resolution, access grants, audit workflows, or asset delivery should remain explicit domain tools even if they call DataFn internally.

+# McpFn architecture
+
+McpFn separates protocol correctness from product correctness.
+
+```text
+MCP client
+   |
+official MCP SDK transports and protocol lifecycle
+   |
+McpFnServer -> trusted request context
+   |
+McpFnRegistry -> input validation -> domain handler -> output validation
+   |                                      |
+explicit domain tool                 DatafnExecutor
+                                          |
+                             DataFn auth, namespace, policy,
+                             hooks, rate limits, idempotency
+```
+
+## Runtime ownership
+
+The official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` owns initialization, JSON-RPC dispatch, stdio framing, Streamable HTTP, capability negotiation, ping, and protocol errors. McpFn does not carry a second MCP protocol implementation.
+
+`McpFnServer` owns server identity, request-context construction, tool dispatch, error normalization, and transport connection lifecycle. One `McpFnServer` instance connects to one transport. A host accepting multiple connections creates one server instance per connection while sharing the immutable registry.
+
+`McpFnRegistry` owns the application contract. Registration rejects duplicate or invalid tool names, empty descriptions, non-object input schemas, and invalid JSON Schemas. Arguments are validated with Ajv before the domain handler runs. Declared output schemas validate `structuredContent` after the handler returns. A domain package may provide `handleInvalidArguments` when it must retain an existing error envelope, as ProbeFn does.
+
+## Manifest compatibility
+
+`createManifest` emits canonical, sorted tool definitions and a SHA-256 hash. `diffManifests` classifies changes as:
+
+- `breaking`: removed tools/properties/support, narrowed enums, tighter constraints, newly required inputs, incompatible output requiredness;
+- `additive`: added tools or optional properties, wider enums, relaxed constraints, added protocol/transport support;
+- `behavioral`: titles, descriptions, or annotations that can alter model tool selection without changing JSON validity.
+
+The diff is deliberately structural. Semantic scenarios are still required for authorization decisions, version resolution, idempotency, side effects, error envelopes, and result meaning.
+
+## DataFn integration
+
+`DatafnServer.executor` is an in-process boundary over the same query, mutation, transaction, and search handlers used by HTTP. It preserves authorization callbacks, namespace and actor derivation, schema permissions, plugins, rate limits, payload limits, and DataFn error envelopes.
+
+`@mcpfn/datafn` consumes that executor. It never accepts tenant, principal, namespace, or DataFn `clientId` values as tool arguments. Reads default on only after a resource is explicitly exposed; writes never default on.
+
+## Security invariants
+
+- Treat names, descriptions, annotations, schemas, and output shapes as versioned public contracts.
+- Build trusted context from the transport/authentication layer, not model-provided arguments.
+- Keep `additionalProperties: false` unless unknown keys are an intentional contract.
+- Prefer explicit output schemas for stable consumers.
+- Mark destructive and read-only annotations accurately; they influence client UX but do not replace server authorization.
+- Do not expose DataFn fields that its resolved read/write capabilities reject.

+# Testing and CI
+
+A regression-free MCP project needs four independent layers.
+
+| Layer | What it catches | McpFn surface |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Unit/domain | Handler logic, authorization, persistence, policy | Existing package tests |
+| Contract | Tool inventory, schemas, descriptions, annotations, advertised support | Hashed manifest plus `mcpfn diff` |
+| Semantic protocol | Real client/server calls and stable business envelopes | `@mcpfn/testing` scenarios |
+| Protocol conformance | Initialization, JSON-RPC, transport, and MCP specification behavior | Official `@modelcontextprotocol/conformance` via `mcpfn conformance` |
+
+## Contract baseline
+
+Generate a candidate manifest from a module whose default export is a `McpFnServer`, an async factory returning one, a `McpFnRegistry`, or an existing manifest:
+
+```sh
+mcpfn manifest ./mcp-server.ts --output ./candidate.manifest.json
+mcpfn diff ./mcpfn.manifest.json ./candidate.manifest.json --fail-on-behavioral
+```
+
+For a registry export, pass both `--name` and `--version`. Exit code `1` means the diff found a breaking change, or a behavioral change when requested. Exit code `2` means the source or command was invalid.
+
+Review additive changes before replacing the committed baseline. A compatible diff means old inputs remain structurally accepted; it does not prove the new tool is authorized or semantically correct.
+
+## Semantic scenarios
+
+```ts
+import type { McpFnScenario } from "@mcpfn/testing";
+
+export default [
+  {
+    name: "resolves the published version",
+    tool: "skill_get",
+    arguments: { slug: "work-linear-issue" },
+    expect: {
+      isError: false,
+      structuredContent: {
+        skill: { slug: "work-linear-issue", version: 3 },
+      },
+      structuredTextParity: true,
+    },
+  },
+] satisfies McpFnScenario[];
+```
+
+`mcpfn test` connects an official client and server with the official in-memory transport. It first checks `tools/list` exactly against the manifest and then runs scenarios serially, returning a JSON report. Use `verify(result)` for assertions that cannot be expressed as exact structured content.
+
+`structuredTextParity` is appropriate only when the text block is JSON representing the same object as `structuredContent`. Human-readable text such as MemoryFn's search summary should be asserted separately.
+
+## Official conformance
+
+Start a real Streamable HTTP endpoint, then run:
+
+```sh
+mcpfn conformance http://127.0.0.1:3000/mcp --suite active
+```
+
+McpFn delegates to the official conformance npm package and returns its exit code. Use an expected-failures file only for reviewed, time-bounded exceptions; do not turn new failures into a silent baseline update.
+

+```sh
+npm run gate:mcpfn-release
+```

+# Migrating an MCP server to McpFn
+
+## 1. Remove hand-written protocol dispatch
+
+Keep domain handlers and schemas, but replace custom `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, ping, stdio framing, and SSE parsing with an `McpFnRegistry` and `McpFnServer`. The official SDK owns those protocol paths.
+
+## 2. Register the existing public contract
+
+Preserve tool names and descriptions unless the change is intentional. Use object JSON Schemas, declare `additionalProperties`, add accurate annotations, and add output schemas wherever consumers rely on structured results.
+
+Handlers should return MCP `CallToolResult` values. `structuredResult` emits both `structuredContent` and an equivalent JSON text block. Existing domain errors with a string `code` retain that code. Use `handleInvalidArguments` only when a package has an established validation envelope that must remain stable.
+
+## 3. Build trusted context
+
+Use `createMcpFnServer({ context })` to derive principals, workspace/tenant IDs, credentials, and request metadata from authenticated transport state. Never copy these values out of tool arguments.
+
+## 4. Replace custom test clients
+
+Use `McpFnTestClient` or an official SDK `Client`. Assert the real initialize and tool-call boundary, not `registry.callTool` or handler functions alone.
+
+## 5. Commit the regression contract
+
+Generate a manifest, review it, add semantic scenarios, and run official conformance for the deployed Streamable HTTP endpoint. Put manifest diff and scenarios in required CI.
+
+## Existing Superfunctions migrations
+
+- LangFn retains its `MCPServer`, `MCPClient`, `StdioMCPTransport`, and `SSEMCPTransport` names at the compatibility edge, but all protocol lifecycle now uses the official SDK. The legacy SSE class name now means Streamable HTTP.
+- MemoryFn's `MemoryMCP` exposes the same two tool names with validated inputs and structured results through McpFn.
+- ProbeFn shares its existing Zod schemas and exact `ProbefnEnvelope` results with McpFn. Its stdio path is official SDK stdio; its optional TCP compatibility transport implements only stream framing and delegates all JSON-RPC/MCP behavior to the SDK server.
+
